title: Mass Spectrometry Proteomics Data Preprocessing
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter covers the import, exploration, and preprocessing of bottom-up, label-free mass spectrometry (MS) proteomics data. We examine how to handle raw peptide intensity outputs, address missing values, apply variance-stabilizing logarithmic transformations, and perform quality control checks prior to statistical testing. ## The CPTAC Benchmark Dataset Quantitative label-free proteomics experiments require rigorous data preprocessing before downstream differential abundance analysis. In this case study, we examine a subset of the Clinical Proteomic Technology Assessment for Cancer (CPTAC) Study 6 benchmark dataset. The experimental design is an artificial spike-in experiment. A fixed protein background consisting of $60\text{ ng}/\mu\text{L}$ *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (yeast, strain BY4741) was spiked with the Sigma Universal Protein Standard mixture 1 (UPS1). The UPS1 mixture comprises 48 human proteins spiked at defined concentrations. Two specific spike-in conditions are compared: - **Condition 6A**: $0.25\text{ fmol}/\mu\text{L}$ of UPS1 proteins in yeast background - **Condition 6B**: $0.74\text{ fmol}/\mu\text{L}$ of UPS1 proteins in yeast background The data were acquired on an LTQ-Orbitrap W instrument at testing site 56, with three technical replicates per condition (runs 7, 8, and 9 for both 6A and 6B). Because the yeast background is kept constant, the true fold change between condition 6B and condition 6A for background yeast proteins is: $$\log_2(\text{FC}_{\text{yeast}}) = \log_2(1) = 0$$ For the spiked-in human UPS1 proteins, the expected concentration ratio is $0.74 / 0.25 = 2.96$, corresponding to an expected $\log_2$ fold change of: $$\log_2(\text{FC}_{\text{UPS1}}) = \log_2(2.96) \approx 1.565$$ Raw MS spectra were identified and quantified using MaxQuant (version 1.5.2.8). The output includes two central tabular files: `peptides.txt` (peptide-level intensities across runs) and `proteinGroups.txt` (protein inference groups and annotation flags). ## Data Architecture and Import The peptide intensities are stored in `peptides.txt`. We use the Bioconductor packages `MSnbase` and `MSqRob`, alongside the `tidyverse` and `limma`, to load and manipulate the data structures. In `MSnbase`, quantitative proteomics experiments are represented using the `MSnSet` container. An `MSnSet` synchronizes three core matrices: 1. `exprs(object)`: An assay matrix containing feature abundances (peptides or proteins as rows, samples as columns). 2. `fData(object)`: A feature metadata dataframe (rows match the rows of `exprs`). 3. `pData(object)`: A phenotypic metadata dataframe describing experimental conditions (rows match the columns of `exprs`). ```r library(MSqRob) library(MSnbase) library(tidyverse) library(limma) peptidesFile <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/statOmics/pda/data/quantification/cptacAvsB_lab3/peptides.txt" proteinGroupsFile <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/statOmics/pda/data/quantification/cptacAvsB_lab3/proteinGroups.txt" # Locate the columns containing intensity measurements ecols <- grepEcols(peptidesFile, "Intensity ", split = "\t") # Import the data into an MSnSet container pepData <- readMSnSet2(peptidesFile, ecol = ecols, fnames = "Sequence", sep = "\t") ``` The resulting `pepData` object contains 11,466 features (unique peptide sequences) across 6 samples: ``` MSnSet (storageMode: lockedEnvironment) assayData: 11466 features, 6 samples element names: exprs protocolData: none phenoData: none featureData featureNames: AAAAGAGGAGDSGDAVTK AAAALAGGK ... YYTVFDRDNNRVGFAEAAR (11466 total) fvarLabels: Sequence N.term.cleavage.window ... MS.MS.Count (65 total) ``` Inspecting the raw expression matrix reveals feature intensities and column header formats: ```r head(exprs(pepData)) ``` ``` Intensity.6A_7 Intensity.6A_8 Intensity.6A_9 Intensity.6B_7 Intensity.6B_8 Intensity.6B_9 AAAAGAGGAGDSGDAVTK 0 0 66760 0 37436 0 AAAALAGGK 2441300 1220000 1337600 2850900 935580 1606200 AAAALAGGKK 1029200 668040 638990 777030 641270 562840 AAADALSDLEIK 515460 670780 712140 426580 620510 737780 AAADALSDLEIKDSK 331130 420900 365560 329250 380820 414490 AAAEEFQR 0 0 51558 0 0 76970 ``` ## Annotation and Feature Filtering ### Sample Metadata Setup The default sample names inherited from MaxQuant (`Intensity.6A_7`, `Intensity.6A_8`, etc.) contain the experimental design. We clean the sample labels and define the experimental factor in `pData`: ```r sampleNames(pepData) <- pepData %>% sampleNames() %>% str_replace(pattern = "Intensity.6", replacement = "") # Define condition factor (A vs B) pData(pepData)$condition <- pepData %>% sampleNames() %>% substr(1, 1) %>% as.factor() ``` ### Feature Metadata Selection The raw `peptides.txt` file contains over 60 annotation fields per peptide. We restrict `fData` to essential tracking variables: protein mapping (`Proteins`), potential contaminants (`Potential.contaminant`), decoy matches (`Reverse`), and the peptide sequence (`Sequence`): ```r pepData <- selectFeatureData( pepData, fcol = c("Proteins", "Potential.contaminant", "Reverse", "Sequence") ) ``` ### Handling Zero Values and Missingness In mass spectrometry, an intensity of `0` denotes an undetected signal—a missing value—rather than a true abundance of zero. We compute the number of non-zero observations per peptide and recast `0` to `NA`: ```r fData(pepData)$nNonZero <- rowSums(exprs(pepData) > 0) exprs(pepData)[exprs(pepData) == 0] <- NA ``` We evaluate the pattern of missingness using the `plotNA()` function from `MSnbase`: ```r plotNA(pepData) ``` In this dataset, approximately 45% of all peptide intensity values are missing. The missingness rate is uniform across all six runs, but several peptides fail to record a single non-zero measurement across all samples. These missing measurements stem from two primary mechanisms: 1. **Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)** / **Missing at Random (MAR)**: Stochastic loss due to precursor ion selection in data-dependent acquisition (DDA). 2. **Missing Not at Random (MNAR)**: Censoring driven by the limit of detection (LOD) of the mass spectrometer, where low-abundance peptides fall below the instrument sensitivity threshold. ## Logarithmic Transformation Raw peptide intensities span several orders of magnitude ($10^4$ to $>10^8$). Density estimation on the raw intensity matrix highlights extreme right-skewness: ```r plotDensities(exprs(pepData)) ``` In raw intensities, the variance of repeated measurements scales proportionally with the mean intensity: $$\text{Var}(Y) \propto E[Y]^2$$ This heteroscedasticity violates the assumption of constant variance (homoscedasticity) required by standard linear statistical models. Applying a base-2 logarithmic transformation achieves two objectives: 1. **Variance stabilization**: It decouples measurement variance from signal intensity, yielding roughly homoscedastic errors across the dynamic range. 2. **Multiplicative to additive scale**: Multiplicative dilution and abundance effects become additive linear shifts on the log scale: $$y_{ijk} = \log_2(Y_{ijk})$$ where differences between sample means directly represent $\log_2$ fold changes: $$\log_2(\text{FC}) = \log_2\left(\frac{Y_B}{Y_A}\right) = \log_2(Y_B) - \log_2(Y_A)$$ We apply the transformation using base 2: ```r pepData <- log(pepData, base = 2) plotDensities(exprs(pepData)) ``` Following the $\log_2$ transformation, the intensity distributions display approximately symmetric, bell-shaped profiles suitable for linear modeling, though minor differences in sample-level location and scale remain to be addressed in subsequent normalization steps. ## Sources - Notes: `CptacAvsB lab3.nb Part 01 —` (Section 1: Background, Section 2: Data, Section 2.1: Data exploration, and Section 3.1: Log transform the data). - The document references Goeminne et al. (2016) [1] and Paulovich et al. [5] regarding MaxQuant search settings and CPTAC Study 6 design details; these papers were referenced in the text but not provided in full.
